questions.title: Two solvents for a plant extract
questions.stem:
The same extract and pure standards P and Q are run on polar silica with two different mobile phases. Distances are measured from the baseline. Rf is spot distance divided by solvent-front distance. Spots U and V belong to the extract; each lane is developed under the stated common conditions.

| Run | Front / cm | P / cm | Q / cm | U / cm | V / cm |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I | 8.0 | 2.0 | 5.6 | 2.0 | 5.6 |
| II | 6.0 | 1.8 | 4.2 | 1.8 | 3.0 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate Rf values for V and Q in each run.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Assess the identifications U=P and V=Q, using both runs.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Within run I, compare how the phases affect P and Q. Explain why absolute migration distances alone cannot be compared between the two runs.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Predict the effect of submerging the starting spots. State one further practical precaution for obtaining reliable Rf values.

steps.text: In run I both V and Q give 5.6/8.0=0.70.
In run II V gives 3.0/6.0=0.50 and Q gives 4.2/6.0=0.70.
Rf is a distance ratio from the same baseline and has no units.
U matches P in both runs (0.25 and 0.30); this supports but does not prove identity.
V matches Q in run I but not in run II, evidence against V=Q.
Different compounds can co-migrate under one set of conditions; a co-run or independent technique gives stronger evidence.
P travels less relative to the front; it is more strongly retained by silica relative to its affinity for that mobile phase.
Q travels further and partitions relatively more into the mobile phase.
Front distances and solvent compositions differ between the runs; the migration balance and distance scale change.
Sample may dissolve into the solvent reservoir and lose its defined starting point.
Mark the front immediately on removal before evaporation; accept use of a pencil baseline, small spots or a level plate.

questions.title: Standardizing a monoprotic acid
questions.stem:
A student dissolves 1.325 g of dry Na₂CO₃ (M=106.0 g mol⁻¹) and makes the solution to 250.0 cm³. A 25.00 cm³ aliquot is titrated with HCl to complete reaction, forming CO₂ and water. Each burette reading has absolute uncertainty ±0.05 cm³.

| Trial | Initial / cm³ | Final / cm³ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rough | 0.00 | 25.40 |
| 1 | 0.10 | 25.00 |
| 2 | 0.30 | 25.25 |
| 3 | 0.15 | 25.05 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the three accurate titres and their mean. Explain the treatment of the rough trial.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the concentration of the sodium carbonate solution and the amount in each aliquot.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Write the ionic equation and determine the HCl concentration.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Estimate the maximum percentage uncertainty from the two burette readings for a single accurate titre. Explain why close titres do not rule out a calibration error.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Suppose the carbonate had absorbed water before weighing. Deduce the direction of error in the calculated acid concentration if the full mass is treated as anhydrous.

steps.text: Accurate titres: 24.90, 24.95 and 24.90 cm³.
Mean=24.9167 cm³, reported as 24.92 cm³.
The rough run locates the endpoint and is not included; the three accurate titres agree within 0.05 cm³.
Aliquot contains 0.05000×0.02500=0.001250 mol.
CO₃²⁻+2H⁺→CO₂+H₂O.
The aliquot consumes 0.002500 mol HCl.
Add reading uncertainties to get ±0.10 cm³ per titre.
A consistent calibration offset in delivered volume can affect all runs similarly, so precision alone does not establish accuracy.
